latin: Cum omnis res ab imperatore delegata intentiorem<sup>1</sup> exigat<sup>2</sup> curam, sitque nunc mihi a Nerva Augusto<sup>3</sup>, nescio diligentiore an amantiore rei publicae imperatore<sup>4</sup>,
aquarum injunctum officium, cum ad usum tum ad salubritatem atque etiam securitatem urbis pertinens<sup>5</sup>,
primum ac potissimum existimo<sup>6</sup>, sicut in ceteris negotiis institueram, nosse quod suscepi<sup>7</sup>.
Quapropter<sup>8</sup> hujus commentarii pertinebit fortassis<sup>9</sup> et ad successorem utilitas,
sed cum inter initia administrationis meae scriptus sit, in primis ad meam institutionem regulamque<sup>10</sup> proficiet...
...Agrippa<sup>11</sup> Virginem<sup>12</sup> in agro Lucullano collectam Romam perduxit.
Virgo adpellata est quod quaerentibus aquam militibus virguncula<sup>13</sup> venas quasdam monstravit,
quas secuti, qui foderant, ingentem aquae modum invenerunt.
Concipitur<sup>14</sup> Virgo palustribus locis, signino<sup>15</sup> circumjecto continendarum scaturiginum<sup>16</sup> causa...
...Ductus Anionis novi efficit passuum quinquaginta octo milia septingentos, ex eo, rivo subterraneo passuum quadraginta novem milia trecentos,
et propius urbem opere arcuato<sup>17</sup> passuum sex milia quadringentos nonaginta unum.
Hi sunt arcus altissimi, sublevati in quibusdam locis pedes centum novem.
Tot aquarum tam multis necessariis molibus pyramidas<sup>18</sup> videlicet otiosas compares, aut cetera inertia sed fama celebrata graecorum!
english: As every [function] (thing) delegated by the Emperor requires a [particularly] (more) attentive care, and as now has been [entrusted to me] by Nerva (Augustus), an emperor [of whom] I do not know [whether he is] more devoted or more friendly to the State,
(entrusted) the administration of the waters, which concerns as much the utility as the hygiene and also the safety of the city,
I consider [it of the] first and [the] principal [importance], as I had decided to do [in my] other activities, [to] know what I have undertaken.
So the utility of this book will perhaps interest also (to) [my] successor,
but as it was written during the beginning(s) of my administration, [it is] in first [place] to my instruction and to my line of conduct [that] it will be of profit...
...Agrippa brought to Rome [the water of the source of] the Virgin, collected in a [property] (field) of Lucullus.
It is called the «Virgin» because, (to) [some] soldiers looking for water, a little girl [showed them] certain [veins] (veins),
which [they followed] (having followed) [so that those] who had dug found an enormous quantity of water.
The «Virgin» [rises] in [a] marshy region, cement having been poured around [in order to] contain the bubbling sources...
...The conduit of the New Anio [is] 58,700 (of) paces [long], of which 49,300 paces in underground canal,
and nearer to the city 6,491 paces [on arches] (by arched work).
These are very high arches, rising in certain places to 109 feet [above the ground].

To [masses] (of waters) so numerous and so necessary [compare] (2nd pers. sg. subj. pres.) the Pyramids for example [and they will appear] useless, or again the other unproductive works of the Greeks, though celebrated by renown!

footnotes: Intentus, -a, -um (p.p.p. of intendere, to stretch towards), applied, eager. Here, its comparative (intentiorem) relates to curam, the noun of which it is an epithet solidly framing the verb exigat (subj.).
Exigo, -is, -ere, egi, actum: 1° to expel (first sense of agere, to push); 2° to carry out completely (sense derived from the same verb); 3° to claim, to exact (cf. fr. exact).
Nerva (ae) Augustus, the emperor Nerva, born in 22, emperor from 96 to 98. Frontinus (35-104) distinguished himself successively as military chief and as civil administrator.

Imperatore and the two comparatives in the ablative (in e and not in i like the adj.) relate to Nerva, complement of agent of injunctum sit (here sit... injunctum) perfect of injungere (to charge with..., to enjoin). This last verb has as its subject officium (pertinens, etc.), a charge (reported).

The whole P. 1-P. 2 is a double adverbial clause introduced by the first cum (P. 1) and whose two verbs (subj. pres.) are exigat and injunctum sit. — Cum... tum (P. 2), not only... but above all; it is a pair of conjunctions that should be known.

Existimo is the main verb of the whole P. 1, P. 2, P. 3; it has as its object P. 1., whose verb (esse) is understood; the logical subject is nosse, infinitive which itself has as its object the relative clause (id) quod suscepi, and the predicate primum ac potissimum. — Potissimus, -a, -um (superlative of potis, -e, which can, used only in the nominative and with esse, e.g. potis es, you can), the principal, the best.
Suscipio, -is, -ere, cepi, ceptum, to undertake (sub + capere).
Quapropter, adv., for this reason.
Fortasse or fortassis, adv., perhaps, about, approximately; from fors, fortis, f., chance (cf. forsan, forsit, forsitan, perhaps).

Regula, -ae, f., ruler for drawing or rule of conduct (regere); one could designate the rail; just a return to Latin, for the English «rail» comes from the Old French raille (bar) which came itself from regula.
Agrippa, -ae, m. (63-12 B.C.), another soldier, contemporary of Augustus, and who was also a builder.
Virginem: each aqueduct had its name; this one was called the Virgo (cf. L. 40, N. 7), you are going to know why (P. 7).
Virguncula, -ae, f.: diminutive of the previous one.
Concipio, -is, -ere, cepi, ceptum, to take, in the sense of to receive (vela ventum concipiunt, the sails take the wind), to contain, to conceive, to engender; whence, in the passive, to take birth.
Signinus, -a, -um: from Signia, a town famous for its mortar. Opus signinum, concrete work, cement masonry.
Scaturigo, -inis, f., gushing spring (scatere, to gush, to bubble). The spring, in general, is said fons, fontis, m.
Opus arcuatum, w. f. w., the work in arches: it is the one that corresponds to the classical aqueduct of engravings. In L. 94 our tourist had therefore taken an aqueduct for a viaduct.
Pyramis, -idis, f. (pr. puramiss): Greek noun, follows the 3rd declension but with the accusative plural in as instead of es. You can forget this detail for the form in es is also acceptable.
comments: We give you here extracts from a book by Frontinus, on the one hand for reasons of vocabulary, on the other hand because we think it may be interesting for you to touch from close a document which informs us directly on a few details of the administration and of Roman civilization. This will allow you at the same time to see that the nature of administrative problems has hardly changed in 2000 years. The title is: De aquae ductu, on the act of leading the water (in a broader sense than the fr. aqueduc) urbis Romae, of the city of Rome.
The indications in Roman numerals, which correspond to the 130 divisions of the original, will give you an idea of the audacious cutting to which we have given ourselves up.

EXERCISE. — To begin to train you in cursive reading, that is to say in current reading, like that of a novel written in our language, we are giving you to read the continuation of PLINY THE YOUNGER, with which we made contact in lesson 97, trying not to look at the translation and the notes until a second reading. — From our special correspondent (end).

If, having reached the end of this first cursive reading, you have the impression of not having understood much, do not despair for all that, and begin such exercises again often. You will have had to read many books for current reading in your mother tongue to become a completely natural act. Do not forget that it is the same in all the other languages.

latin: Nec multo post, illa nubes descendere in terras, operire<sup>1</sup> maria;
cinxerat Capreas et absconderat<sup>2</sup>.
Jam cinis<sup>3</sup>, adhuc tamen rarus.
Respicio<sup>4</sup>: densa caligo<sup>5</sup> tergis imminebat, quae nos torrentis modo infusa<sup>6</sup> terrae sequebatur.
Audires ululatus<sup>7</sup> feminarum, infantium quiritatus<sup>8</sup>, clamores virorum.
Alii parentes, alii liberos, alii conjuges<sup>9</sup> vocibus requirebant, vocibus noscitabant<sup>10</sup>.
Hi suum casum, illi suorum miserabantur<sup>11</sup>; erant qui metu mortis mortem precarentur<sup>12</sup>.
Paulum reluxit<sup>13</sup>, quod non dies nobis, sed adventantis<sup>14</sup> ignis indicium videbatur.
Et ignis quidem longius substitit<sup>15</sup>; tenebrae rursus<sup>16</sup>, cinis rursus, multus et gravis.
Hunc identidem<sup>17</sup> adsurgentes<sup>18</sup> excutiebamus<sup>19</sup>; operti alioqui<sup>20</sup> atque etiam oblisi<sup>21</sup> pondere essemus.
Tandem illa caligo tenuata<sup>22</sup> quasi in fumum nebulamve excessit.
Mox dies verus; sol etiam effulsit<sup>23</sup>, luridus<sup>24</sup> tamen, qualis esse, cum deficit, solet.
Occursabant trepidantibus adhuc oculis mutata omnia altoque cinere tanquam nive obducta.
Regressi tamen Misenum curatisque utcumque<sup>25</sup> corporibus, suspensam dubiamque noctem spe ac metu exegimus.
english: And [a little] (not much) after, this cloud [descended] towards the land, [covered] the sea(s).
It had surrounded and hidden Capri.
Already the ash, still rare however.
I look behind me: a thick black cloud threatened (dos, dat. pl.) [behind us] which followed us in the manner of a torrent poured over the earth.
You would have heard the howling of women, the cries of babies, the shouts of men.
Some [cried after] their parents, others [after] their children, others [after] their spouses (or wives) (by the voices they asked), sought to recognize one another by [the] (their) voices.
The latter deplored their own misfortune, the former [that] of their own; there were some who, for fear of death, went as far as to implore death.
The light came back a little, which did not appear to us as [being] the day, but as the sign of the fire which was approaching.
And the fire however stopped quite far (= remained at a distance); once again the darkness, once again the ash, abundant and heavy.
This [ash] at several reprises [we shook off by rising] (rising we shook it off); otherwise we would have been covered and even crushed by the weight.
Finally this obscurity having weakened went away as in smoke or in a cloud.
Soon the true day; the sun even shone, pale however, such as it usually is [during an eclipse] (when it fails).
[There presented themselves before] our eyes still trembling [the] objects transformed and covered with a thick ash as if by snow.
Having returned however to Misenum and [having] in any case [cleaned ourselves] (the bodies having been), we passed an anxious and uncertain night between hope and fear.
footnotes: Descendere, operire, are so-called infinitives of narration (cf. GRAMMATICAL APPENDIX, § 65). Their subject is in the nominative, for they have nothing to do with an infinitive clause.

Abscondo, -is, -ere, condi, conditum, to place far from looks, to hide. — Capreae, -arum, f., the island of Capri (now Capri), to the south of Naples. Capra, -ae, f., the goat; the billy-goat: caper, -pri or hircus, -i.
Cinis, -eris, m. (cf. L. 24, N. 7).

Respicere, to look behind oneself. We have already seen aspicere (L. 9). This family is very numerous: conspicere, circum-, di-, de-, in-, per-, pro-, suspicere; know simply how to recognize their kinship (specio, to look, practically disappeared verb, but which left species, -ei, f., the aspect, then the species); if you need to know the precise sense of one of them, refer to your dictionary or, better, to a methodical vocabulary.
Caligo, -inis, m. (cf. L. 79, N. 8).
Infusa: perfect passive participle of infundo, -is, -ere, fudi, fusum, to pour in, to spread; it relates to caligo; note its complement terrae in the dative.
Ululatus, -us, m., from ululare, to howl (animals), to utter piercing cries.

Likewise quiritare, lit., to call the citizens to help (quirites, -ium or -um, m.), to be compared with quaeritare, frequentative of quaerere, to ask. We have followed the indicated text, but it seems to us that neither of these two verbs suits the case of babies (infans, cf. L. 51, N. 3).
Conjux, conjugis, m. and f., spouse.
Noscitare, to seek to know, frequentative of noscere (one rather employs nosse = novisse).

Miserari (1st conj.), to lament, to deplore, to express one's pity; not to be confused with misereor, -eris, -eri, miseritus sum, to have pity on + genitive. Do you know its imperative and the expression: miserere nostri, have pity on us (pl. miseremini)? N.B. — The dative nobis, although better known, is less classical than the genitive nostri.

Precari, to pray or to wish: precari aliquid ab aliquo, to implore something of someone; alicui bona precari, to wish someone well. Note that, in P. 7, this verb is in the subjunctive (impf.); it is the rule called sunt qui + subj.: there are some (people who go as far as to do...).
Relucescere (pft reluxi), to shine again, inchoative verb; relucere (same perfect), to reflect, to shine again.
Adventare, to approach; (is constructed with ad, sub or in + acc.), to advance.
Subsisto, -is, -ere, stiti, v.i., to stop, to remain, to resist; in itinere subsistere, to remain on the way.
Rursus, adv., backwards, again.
Identidem, at several reprises.
(As)surgo or (ad)surgo, -is, -ere, surrexi, surrectum, to rise (towards, for).
Excutio, -is, -ere, cussi, cussum, to make leave by shaking (cf. percutere, same conjugation, to strike, to pierce by striking, like the percussor of a rifle).
Alioqui or alioquin, otherwise.
Oblido, -is, -ere, isi, isum, to squeeze, to stifle; from laedo, -is, -ere, laesi, laesum, to wound, to damage (cf. fr. léser).
Tenuare, to diminish; the corresponding adjective is tenuis, -e, not very thick, thin.
Effulgere, to come out shining (cf. L. 97, N. 23).
Luridus, -a, -um, of a pale yellow; luror, -oris, colour or yellowish complexion.
Utcumque, in any manner whatever, in any case.
